Issued at 140 PM CDT Wed Oct 7 2026

QUIET WEATHER THE NEXT FEW DAYS...Early afternoon upper-level 
analysis displays troughing over the Great Lakes and large scale
ridging over the western CONUS. The Upper Midwest is placed 
between these two features within a belt of enhanced northwesterly
flow (50+ knot 700mb winds), which mixes down as 20-30 mph surface
gusts through the afternoon across central MN and western WI. 
Satellite reveals abundant sunshine over the forecast area and 
highs in the upper 60s (north) to mid 70s (south) are on track.
Should also note that mixing of the air mass will result in 
afternoon dew points falling into the upper 30s, which yields 
minimum RH's between 25-35 percent. The combination of dry air 
and breezy northwest winds supports the mention of elevated fire
weather conditions through this afternoon. High pressure expands
southeastward tonight and will set the stage for another night 
in the 40s. Tranquil weather is on deck for Thursday, with 
slightly cooler highs in the upper 60s, light winds, and mid to 
high clouds increasing through the day. 

NEAR CRITICAL FIRE WEATHER CONDITIONS LIKELY SATURDAY...Changes are 
on the way heading into the weekend as a strong mid-level low 
tracks across southern Canada Friday through Sunday. Friday 
serves as the transition day, with the potential for a few early
day showers or a storm across far southern MN in association 
with the nocturnal LLJ (likely oriented to the southeast into 
eastern IA). We'll likely have a cloudy start to the day with 
mid-level WAA underway. Skies clear from south to north as the 
surface front surges north, which will result in widespread 
highs in the 70s Friday afternoon (warmest along I-90). The 
warmth really ramps up on Saturday as the surface pressure 
gradient tightens south and east of developing ~990s mb surface 
low set to exist over the Dakotas. In the mid-levels, a 
seasonably strong 50-55kt southwesterly jet will span from 
southwest to northeast across the forecast area, which supports 
the advection of an anomalously warm air mass characterized by 
20-21C 850mb T's (which is a roughly 12-16C temperature anomaly
for the start of the second week of October!). Widespread 
afternoon highs in the mid 80s are likely -- though the current 
forecast high of 85 at MSP would fall short of the daily record 
of 90 (1928) which also happens to be the latest 90 recorded in 
the Twin Cities. In addition to the warmth, the strong mid-level
flow and mixing of the air mass will support a very windy day 
with sustained winds between 20-30 mph and gusts upwards up 
40-45 mph. Despite modest moisture advection (dew points 
climbing back into the mid 50s by midday Saturday), the degree 
of surface heating will drop minimum afternoon RH's to between 
30-35 percent, which combines with the strong southerly winds to
support near critical fire weather conditions. Should temperatures
warm more than forecast, the increase in the vapor pressure 
deficit (VPD) could result in a critical fire weather scenario 
developing. We have collaborated with neighboring offices to 
boost winds & lower Td's on Saturday to reflect our latest 
forecast thoughts.

COOLER WITH PRECIPITATION CHANCES EARLY NEXT WEEK...By Sunday, 
the synoptic look is quite interesting over the eastern CONUS. 
The mid-level low responsible for our significant warm up will 
have translated east across Ontario/north of the Great Lakes. 
Regional attention will be on the northward advance of the 
remnants of T.S Isaias, which are progged to travel north into 
the Ohio Valley. With the mid-level low exiting to the east and 
tropical moisture progged to remain southeast of the Upper 
Midwest, Sunday should be another dry and warm day with highs 
in the upper 70s to lower 80s. While still breezy at times, 
southwesterly winds will not be nearly as strong as Saturday. 
Still, with warm temperatures and breezy winds it's possible 
that elevated fire weather conditions persist through Sunday 
afternoon. The warmth ends as a strong cold front comes crashing
south Sunday evening, turning the winds northwesterly and ushering
in a much cooler air mass. High temperatures fall into the 
50s/lower 60s and lows in the upper 30s/lower 40s for the first 
half of next week. Following a dry frontal passage, a quick 
hitting disturbance across the northern Plains will bring the 
potential for light rain on Monday, as represented by 30-50% 
PoPs from the latest NBM. Forecast confidence in precipitation 
trends drops after Monday, due to temporal uncertainties 
surrounding the evolution of tropical cyclone remnants set to
interact with slow-moving western troughing early next week.
